title: Colombia Earthquake Kills 132, Ukraine Strikes Deep Into Russia, Trump Demands War Reparations From Iran
subhead: A magnitude 7.4 quake devastates western Colombia in the country's deadliest seismic event in decades. Ukraine's drone attack on Tatarstan kills at least 13, while Trump's compensation demands on Tehran further stall Hormuz negotiations.

sections.heading: Colombia Hit by Devastating 7.4 Earthquake
sections.body:
A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia at 07:34 local time on Monday, killing at least 132 people and injuring more than 480, according to the BBC and Colombian officials. The quake's epicentre was near San José del Palmar in Chocó province, at a depth of 103km, and was felt across an enormous area stretching hundreds of kilometres — including Bogotá, Cali, Medellín, and as far as Venezuela, Ecuador, and Panama.

The cities of Pereira and Cali suffered the worst damage. At least 40 people died in Pereira's metropolitan area, where 65 buildings collapsed, and people are believed trapped in 15 of them. In Cali, Colombia's third-largest city, 32 buildings collapsed. A curfew is in place in parts of Pereira until 05:00 Tuesday. Several regional airports reported damage, including Pereira, Manizales, and Buenaventura.

Colombia's newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella — who took office only on Friday — declared a national disaster, granting special powers to reallocate budgets. The US, EU, and El Salvador have offered support, with the EU activating its Copernicus satellite for rescue operations. The US Geological Survey estimated 1.5 million people felt shaking close to magnitude seven.
sections.whyItMatters: Colombia faces a humanitarian emergency just days into a new presidency, testing the incoming government's crisis response and exposing the seismic vulnerability of cities in the country's densely populated coffee-growing region.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Drone Strike Reaches 1,200km Into Russia
sections.body:
A Ukrainian drone strike on the city of Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan — over 1,100km from the Ukrainian border — killed at least 13 people, including one child, and injured 75 more, Russian officials confirmed. Seven of the dead were Uzbek citizens, according to the Uzbek consulate. Ukraine's armed forces said the target was the Tanevo oil refinery, one of Russia's largest and most technologically advanced, owned by Tatneft. The same facility was previously hit in June.

Verified footage showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising from the industrial zone, with air raid sirens sounding for hours overnight. Russia's defence ministry said it intercepted 456 Ukrainian drones across Russian territory and annexed Crimea. Separately, an industrial facility in Siberia's Tyumen region was hit by falling drones, and power outages were reported in Novorossiysk, a major Black Sea export port.

The strike ranks among the deadliest Ukrainian attacks on Russian soil since the invasion began, drawing condemnation from Moscow, which called it a terrorist act. Ukraine's Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Centre for Countering Disinformation, said the facilities targeted 'contribute to Russia's war effort,' adding that 'every civilian death in Russia is on Putin.'
sections.whyItMatters: Kyiv is demonstrating it can strike deep into Russia's industrial heartland, forcing Moscow to spread air defences thin and disrupting oil revenue that funds the war — but civilian casualties among migrant workers raise the stakes of this escalatory campaign.

sections.heading: Trump Demands Iran Pay War Reparations as Hormuz Talks Stall
sections.body:
US President Donald Trump said he will demand Iran pay compensation for 'thousands' of US soldier deaths from decades of Iranian-backed attacks, including the USS Cole bombing, as well as for the hundreds of thousands of 'innocent protesters' killed by the Iranian regime over 50 years and the 52,000 he said had been killed in the last five months of war. In a second post on Truth Social, he expanded the demand to include damages for the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza.

The demands came in response to Iranian negotiators making similar claims for damages caused by the US bombing campaign. Trump's statements are the clearest sign yet that negotiations to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse. Despite repeated claims by Trump and senior officials that a deal was imminent, none has materialised in five months of conflict.

According to the Guardian, the compensation demands are effectively a nonstarter for Tehran and further complicate Trump's effort to wind down the conflict ahead of November's midterm elections, where high oil prices and inflation threaten Republican losses.
sections.whyItMatters: Trump's reparations demands signal the Hormuz negotiations are stuck — and the longer they remain so, the more upward pressure on global oil prices and US domestic political risk for Republicans heading into midterms.

sections.heading: Netanyahu Rejects Trump's Gaza Peace Plan as Election Loomoms
sections.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told his cabinet on Sunday that 'Israel does not accept the 15-point document' for Gaza, vowing that the IDF would not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed — 'heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry.' The rejection of the Trump-backed Board of Peace roadmap was a remarkably public break between the leaders of the US and its closest Middle East ally.

However, the White House appears unbothered. A senior US official told Israeli journalist Barak Ravid that 'we understand Bibi's political needs,' framing the rejection as campaign rhetoric ahead of Israel's 27 October general election — the first since the 7 October attacks. Construction of the first International Stabilisation Force base in Rafah is still scheduled to begin this month, according to Israeli public radio.

Board of Peace High Commissioner Nickolay Mladenov, in an interview with Israel's Channel 12, said the plan takes 'a step-by-step approach' built on 'verification, not trust.' Hamas has indicated it remains committed to the roadmap and called on mediators to pressure Israel to comply. Meanwhile, Netanyahu faces an uphill election contest, having failed to deliver the 'absolute victory' he promised over Hamas.
sections.whyItMatters: Netanyahu's rejection is likely tactical — timed for an election audience — but it delays an already fragile process and reveals the tension between Israel's domestic politics and Washington's timeline for a foreign policy win before midterms.

sections.heading: Russia Bans Only Anti-War Party From Parliamentary Elections
sections.body:
A Moscow court barred Yabloko, Russia's only registered liberal and anti-war party, from standing in next month's parliamentary elections. The case was brought by Rodina, a pro-Kremlin nationalist party, which accused Yabloko of supporting an 'extremist organisation' by publishing pro-LGBT content on its website — referencing Russia's 2023 Supreme Court designation of the 'international LGBT movement' as extremist. Rodina also cited copyright infringement over a member quoting Soviet-era song lyrics.

Russia's financial monitoring service claimed Yabloko received foreign money through third parties. Several party members had already been barred from running, including deputy leader Maxim Kruglov, sentenced to seven years in June for social media posts about civilian casualties in Bucha and Mariupol. Yabloko campaigned under the slogan 'For peace and freedom! For a life without fear!'

The BBC reports that United Russia's ratings have fallen to 33% amid inflation, internet blackouts, and drone strikes. Yabloko had been gaining support as the sole anti-war voice on the ballot. With all 10 remaining parties either supporting the war or declining to criticise it, low turnout among opposition voters would likely benefit the Kremlin.
sections.whyItMatters: The ban eliminates the last organised anti-war voice from Russia's ballot, leaving voters no peaceful outlet for opposition and virtually guaranteeing a Kremlin-friendly Duma — even as public dissatisfaction with the war and economic conditions grows.

sections.heading: Record Ocean Temperatures and European Drought Deepen
sections.body:
The world's oceans recorded their hottest July on record, with average sea surface temperatures reaching 20.96°C between 60°N and 60°S — surpassing the previous record of 20.89°C set in 2023, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service. The developing El Niño in the Pacific is forecast to strengthen in coming months, raising the prospect of further temperature records.

Western Europe is experiencing an exceptional run of extreme heat. The average temperature for June and July was 21.62°C — 2.79°C above average and the highest on record for that two-month period. England and Wales had their driest July since records began 190 years ago, with large parts of England and all of Wales now officially in drought. River levels on the Seine, Rhine, and Danube are exceptionally low, threatening water supplies, river transport, and energy production.

July 2026 was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, at 1.47°C above the pre-industrial average. The Met Office's latest assessment found that the hottest day of the year in southern England is now 4.5°C warmer than the 1961–1990 average. Copernicus director Laurence Rouil warned that larger fires are producing smoke that travels further, meaning countries with few wildfires could increasingly be affected.
sections.whyItMatters: The convergence of record ocean temperatures, a strengthening El Niño, and deepening European drought creates compounding risks for agriculture, energy, and water security — with the warmest oceans on record also supercharging tropical storms and raising sea levels.

bottomLine: Colombia's 7.4 earthquake dominated the day with over 130 dead and widespread destruction in the coffee-growing west, testing a brand-new president just days into office. Ukraine demonstrated its deep-strike reach again with a lethal drone attack on Tatarstan, killing at least 13 — while Russia shut down the last anti-war party before next month's Duma elections. Trump's demand that Iran pay war reparations signals the Hormuz negotiations are stuck, compounding domestic pressure from rising oil prices ahead of midterms. Netanyahu's rejection of the Gaza peace plan looks tactical for an October election but delays an already fragile process. And record ocean temperatures coupled with deepening European drought are turning climate stress into a compounding crisis for water, food, and energy security.
